column1: What does the model do in a coding agent?
column2: One thing: text in, text out. It reads no files, runs nothing and remembers nothing between requests.

column1: Raschka's six components of a coding agent?
column2: Live repo context; prompt shape and cache reuse; tool access; minimising context bloat; structured session memory; bounded delegation.

column1: Why keep a fixed prompt prefix?
column2: Identical leading bytes on every request let a server reuse its cached work.

column1: What is the cost of taking the workspace snapshot once at start-up?
column2: It goes stale: files the agent writes do not appear in its status until it restarts.

column1: Who decides whether a tool call runs?
column2: The harness: it checks the tool name, the arguments and the file path, and asks for approval if the tool is risky.

column1: Why does a base GPT-2 answer an agent prompt with prose?
column2: It was never trained on the response format; it continues documents.

column1: What is the Ollama-compatible trick in the GPT-2 project?
column2: The server answers the same API as a popular model runner, so the agent works unchanged against either.

column1: Two datasets in the GPT-2 project, and what each tests?
column2: Instruction pairs (loss on the reply only) test 'it needs the format'; raw code (loss on every token) tests 'it needs more code'.

column1: What does 'correct by construction' mean for training targets?
column2: The script builds the repository first, so it knows the right tool call for any question about it.

column1: Why is HTTP's statelessness important for agents?
column2: The server keeps nothing between requests, so the harness must re-send the whole transcript every turn.
1,024 tokens. A lean agent prompt uses about half before the question is asked.

column1: How is a delegated sub-agent kept safe?
column2: One level deep, read-only, and it returns a single string.
